title: A Living Sacrifice, One Body
sum: With a single "therefore" Paul turns from eleven chapters of what God has done to what the church is to do. The first answer is one verse long: give your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, and let a renewed mind, not the pattern of the age, shape how you think. Then comes the body of Christ, many parts with different gifts, none with a reason to boast.

The rest of the chapter is a string of short commands about love: for one another, for strangers, for persecutors and for enemies. It ends with one of Paul's most quoted lines: "Defeat evil with good." The Romans were a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and householders, and their quarrels (taken up in chapter 14) are never far from view.
readings: As a call to the whole person

Paul asks for the "bodies" of the Romans, their hands, work and daily dealings, not just their feelings or their ideas. The whole chapter is the proof: it is about meals, houses, enemies and neighbors, not about private religion.
As the church's rule of life

Many readers have taken 12:3-21 as a rule for the community: gifts for the common good, love without acting, and a refusal to repay evil. Others read verses 14-21 as advice on how a small, vulnerable group should behave toward the world around it.

views.H: Rome in the winter of 56-57 had several house churches of Jews and Gentiles, and the Jewish believers had come back to the city only a few years before, after the Claudian expulsion (see Acts 18:2). The call not to think too highly of oneself (12:3) and to "go along with the lowly" (12:16) fits churches where slaves and freedpeople met in the homes of wealthier members. The advice not to take revenge (12:19) fits a group that had been pushed out of the city once.
views.C: The chapter is the start of the "paraenesis" (advice) of Romans, and 12:9-21 is built from traditional sayings, many of them from Proverbs and Leviticus, some close to the teaching of Jesus. Critical scholars discuss whether Paul wrote this section for the Romans or drew on a stock of moral instruction. The sayings are loosely strung together, with no clear logic from verse to verse; verses 9-13 look inward, 14-21 outward. The gifts list (12:6-8) differs from 1 Corinthians 12 and is Paul's way of saying that a church needs ordinary service, giving and teaching alongside prophecy.
views.L: Verse 1 uses a verb of appeal ("I appeal to you") that opens a new section, as in 15:30 and 16:17. The chapter is framed by the words "good" and "evil": the will of God is "what is good" (12:2); the last line says to "defeat evil with good" (12:21). Between them the images go from the altar (12:1) to the body (12:4-5) to the battlefield (12:21).
views.J: A Jewish reader will hear the temple in verse 1 and Scripture in nearly every line: Proverbs 3:4, 7 and 25:21-22; Leviticus 19; Deuteronomy 32:35. Paul asks Gentile believers to live by the moral wisdom of Israel's Scriptures, with no rule about circumcision, Sabbath or food in this chapter. The ban on revenge and the call to feed an enemy belong to a long Jewish stream of teaching, which Jesus also drew on.
views.T: Calvin opens his account of the Christian life with Romans 12:1-2: "We are not our own ... we are God's" (Institutes 3.7.1). In the Orthodox liturgy of St John Chrysostom the eucharistic offering is called a "reasonable (logikē) service," after 12:1. Chrysostom's homilies on Romans turn here to practical matters. The Reformers used 12:6 for the "analogy of faith," and Pentecostals look to the gifts list in 12:6-8 together with 1 Corinthians 12 to 14.

deep.b:
The chapter has three parts, each begun with a short appeal or command:

  • 12:1-2 The general appeal: offer yourselves; be changed in mind.
  • 12:3-8 Life in the body: a warning against pride and a list of gifts.
  • 12:9-21 Love in practice: first inside the church (9-13), then toward people who are hostile (14-21).

Several of these lines echo Jesus' teaching, such as blessing persecutors (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28), and Proverbs. Paul does not label them as quotations, which suggests the Romans already knew them. The topic pages on nonviolence and love your neighbor follow the same teaching through the Bible.

deep.title: Why 'heap coals' follows 'Vengeance is mine'
deep.b: Claude's theory: Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 but leaves off the last line of the proverb in its Hebrew and Greek forms, which promises that the LORD will repay the one who feeds his enemy. Dropping it may be deliberate. In 12:19 Paul has just handed all repayment to God, so a promise that you will be repaid would turn kindness into a way of earning something. If so, "coals of fire" means only that the enemy is confronted by goodness, and what comes of it is left in God's hands. This fits readings (1) and (3) of the note at 12:20 and overlaps with the commentaries that stress the context of 12:19 and 12:21; it is not a new reading.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4:1-16; Proverbs 3:4, 7; Proverbs 25:21-22; Deuteronomy 32:35; Leviticus 19:17-18; Matthew 5:38-48; Luke 6:27-36; 1 Peter 3:8-12

settings.what: How the new people of God are to live
settings.to: The Christians in Rome: several house churches of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free
settings.when: from Corinth, in the winter of about 56-57, after eleven chapters on what God has done
settings.why: To turn the letter's long argument into daily life. Having shown that Jews and Gentiles are saved on the same terms and that God has not dropped Israel, Paul asks the Romans to live as one body, to give themselves to God, to love, to deal wisely with the state and to welcome one another across the line between strong and weak.
settings.readers: A church that had been split by the Claudian expulsion and its aftermath, whose Jewish and Gentile members saw some things differently (14:1 to 15:13). Chapters 12 and 13 prepare the ground for the appeal of 15:7: welcome one another.
views: Many commentators read chapters 12 to 13 as general advice that could be sent to any church, and chapter 14 as the specific problem. On this view the sections 12:1-13:14 are 'typical' moral teaching, like what Paul gave in every church.

Others (Wedderburn, Jewett) hold that even the general lines have Rome in mind: the call to stay humble (12:3, 16), to leave revenge (12:19) and to pay taxes (13:6-7) answer fears and quarrels of the Roman house churches.

settings.to: Every member of the Roman house churches, one by one ("every one of you")
settings.when: as part of the appeal that follows the thanksgiving of 11:33-36
settings.why: To check pride and to give each member a place. If the church is one body, no gift is the source of rank. The list of gifts (prophecy, service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leading, mercy) is a list of acts that can be done in a house, which may be why it differs from the more public gifts of 1 Corinthians.
settings.readers: Paul has never been to Rome. He does not name leaders, which may mean the house churches had no single leader.

settings.what: Instructions on love, and on the treatment of enemies
settings.to: The Roman churches, first for dealings among believers (12:9-13), then for dealings with hostile outsiders (12:14-21)
settings.when: as the practical result of the 'therefore' of 12:1
settings.why: To show what 'love without acting' looks like in a city where believers were a small, often suspected minority. Revenge is ruled out because God, not the believer, will judge; the believer's weapon is good.
settings.readers: Believers who had been affected by the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius and who still lived among neighbors who distrusted them.
views: Some read verses 14-21 only as advice on how to meet persecution from outside.
Others hear the quarrel between strong and weak (chapter 14) behind verses 16-18: do not look down on others; keep the peace if you can.

traditions.q: Do prophecy, healing and the other 'gifts' of the Spirit continue today?
views: Yes. All the gifts named in the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues and healing, are given to the church in every age; the baptism in the Holy Spirit is the believer's way into these gifts. The Assemblies of God's Statement of Fundamental Truths holds this.

Yes, in the form of 'charisms,' which the Spirit gives to the faithful, ordinary or remarkable, for building the church. They are to be received with thanks and tested by the church's pastors, whose job is to judge what is genuine (Catechism 799-801; Lumen Gentium 12).

Divided. One line, following B. B. Warfield and the Westminster Confession's statement that God's earlier ways of revealing his will 'are now ceased,' holds that miraculous gifts such as prophecy and tongues ended with the apostolic age. Other Reformed and Presbyterian Christians hold that none of the gifts has ended.

The Spirit's gifts continue in the life of the church, in the sacraments, in saints and holy elders who show discernment, healing and prophecy-like insight. The Orthodox stress that gifts are tested by the church's faith and by love.

Luther taught that God gives the Spirit only through the outward word and the sacraments (Smalcald Articles, part 3, article 8). Lutheran teachers differ on whether the miraculous gifts of the apostolic age continue today.

Classic dispensationalism holds that the 'sign gifts' (tongues, miraculous healing, apostolic prophecy) were given to authenticate the apostles' message and ceased when the New Testament was complete; the Dallas Theological Seminary doctrinal statement is a standard expression of this.

title: Rulers, Debts and the Dawn
sum: Chapter 13 has three parts. The first, 13:1-7, tells the Roman believers to submit to the governing authorities, who are God's servants for good, and to pay what they owe, taxes included. It is the most debated passage in the letter, because it has been used both to defend obedience to unjust rulers and to argue for limits on rulers' power.

The second part (13:8-10) says the only debt to leave unpaid is love, which fulfills the law. The third (13:11-14) urges the church to wake up: the night is nearly over, so "put on the Lord Jesus Christ." That last verse changed Augustine's life, and it is the Epistle in the church's season of Advent.
readings: A rule for all times

On the traditional reading Paul states a general truth about government, that God has put it in place to restrain evil, and so believers owe it respect, taxes and obedience, within the limits set elsewhere in Scripture (Acts 5:29).
A word to Rome in 57

Another reading takes the passage as advice to one church at one moment: Jews and Christians had been expelled once over riots, there was anger over taxes, and Paul wanted the Romans to give the authorities no cause for trouble. Both readings allow that some commands of rulers must be refused.

views.H: Claudius' expulsion of the Jews from Rome (about AD 49) had come from unrest in the Jewish community (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2). In AD 58 the Roman people protested against the tax collectors and Nero considered abolishing indirect taxes (Tacitus, Annals 13.50-51). Paul wrote in the first years of Nero's rule, usually thought to be a calm period; the persecution after the fire of Rome in 64 lay ahead. Roman taxes were both direct (the tribute, phoros) and indirect (customs and tolls, telos), and 13:7 names both.
views.C: Some scholars have proposed that 13:1-7 was not written by Paul but added later (J. Kallas; J. C. O'Neill). There is no manuscript evidence for this, the passage fits its place between 12:21 and 13:8, and almost no one accepts it. A more common discussion is whether Paul meant a general theory of the state or advice for a particular moment, and how the passage fits his own experience of Roman officials and his later execution under Nero. Ernst Käsemann held that the passage must be read against the enthusiasts who thought freedom in Christ meant freedom from all authority.
views.L: 13:1-7 stands between the command to defeat evil with good (12:21) and the command to love (13:8-10). Some see a ring: submit (13:1), fear and honor (13:7), love (13:8). The repeated word "servant" (13:4, twice; 13:6 a related word) and the references to "anger" tie back to 12:19. The dawn image of 13:11-14 closes the section on conduct before the subject changes in chapter 14.
views.J: Jews in the Diaspora had long lived under foreign rulers and had developed ways to pray for them and obey them within limits (Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 2:21; Ezra 6:10; Wisdom 6:1-4). Paul's lines would have been unremarkable to many Roman Jews, and an outright warning to those inclined to rebel: the Jewish revolt against Rome (AD 66-70) was still to come. The summary of the law in Leviticus 19:18 (13:9) is also a Jewish summary: Hillel and Akiva each had a form of it.
views.T: Chrysostom treats the passage as showing that Christianity is no enemy of the empire. Augustine, in the City of God, grounds the state's role in the need to curb sin. Luther's doctrine of two kingdoms rests on Romans 13 (Temporal Authority, 1523); Calvin, with the lesser magistrates, on the same passage (Institutes 4.20). The Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (1934) and the South African Kairos Document (1985) are two modern attempts to say what the passage does not mean. The Anabaptists read it alongside the Sermon on the Mount.

deep.b:
1. A general principle. Government is God's gift for order, and Christians owe it obedience in all that does not contradict God. Most Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed teaching holds this, with limits (see the card).

2. A word for Rome in the 50s. Paul had Rome's tax tension and the memory of the expulsion in mind, and the passage is practical advice for that moment (Dunn, Moo, Jewett differ in detail).

3. A text with an edge. Some scholars (for example, N. T. Wright and Neil Elliott) point out that Paul says rulers are God's servants only so far as they praise the good and punish the evil (13:3-4), which means that a ruler who does the opposite is not doing God's work. On this reading the passage is a limit on the state as well as a charge to believers.

4. An insertion. Because the manuscripts all have it, the theory that Paul did not write it (O'Neill, Kallas) is a small minority view.

Which of these a reader prefers will depend on how they weigh Paul's own life: he was beaten and jailed by Roman officials, he appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and he ended in Roman custody.

deep.h: The dawn, and Augustine in the garden
deep.b: In the late summer of 386 Augustine, a teacher of rhetoric in Milan, was in turmoil in a garden. He wrote later in the Confessions (8.12) that he heard a child's voice from a house nearby, repeating tolle lege, "take up and read." He took up Paul's letters and read the first passage on which his eyes fell. It was Romans 13:13-14. "I did not want to read further, and there was no need," he says (the Plain's own rendering of his Latin). His account made this passage one of the best-known conversion texts in the Christian West. In the same passage Augustine recalls Antony of Egypt, who was moved to give up his goods when he heard the gospel read as if it were said to him (Matthew 19:21).

echoes: Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 2:21; Proverbs 8:15-16; Wisdom 6:1-4; Mark 12:13-17; Acts 5:29; Acts 25:11; Titus 3:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Revelation 13; Leviticus 19:18; Exodus 20:13-17; Galatians 5:14; 1 Thessalonians 5:4-8

settings.what: The duty to the governing authorities
settings.to: The Roman believers, Jews and Gentiles, living in the capital under Nero (54-68), within a few years of the expulsion of the Jews and with tax anger rising
settings.why: To tell believers to be good citizens in a city where the church had a fragile standing: not to rebel, to pay what was due, to honor those in office. The reason given is not fear of punishment but that God has set up the office for good.
settings.readers: A small minority, many of them Jews or former Gentile sympathizers of the synagogues, in the city where the emperor lived.
views: The passage states a general rule about government that applies wherever believers live.
It answers local worries: the memory of the expulsion, the tax protests, and the risk that talk of a coming kingdom of God would sound like treason (compare 13:11-12).
Aimed at believers who thought themselves free
Käsemann read it against believers who took 'freedom in Christ' to mean that earthly authority did not apply to them.

settings.what: Love fulfills the law; the day is near
settings.when: as the close of the section on conduct
settings.why: To sum up the ethics of 12:1-13:7 in one word, love, and give a reason for urgency: the day of the Lord is nearer than when they first believed.
settings.readers: Believers in a city of wild parties and cheap pleasures, and with their own divisions to face (14:1).

traditions.q: Must Christians always obey the government, and when may they resist?
views: Authority comes from God, and obedience is a duty of conscience; but citizens must refuse commands that are against the moral order, and armed resistance to tyranny is allowed only under strict conditions: grave and certain violation of rights, all other ways tried, no worse disorders, real hope of success (Catechism 1897-1904, 2242-2243; Gaudium et Spes 74).

The ideal is 'symphony' between church and state, working in harmony, as in Justinian's Novella 6. Christians are to obey and pray for rulers; but when the state demands what contradicts the faith, the Russian Orthodox Church's Social Concept (2000) says that obedience must be refused, even to martyrdom.

Luther's 'two kingdoms': God rules the world through both the church (by the gospel) and the state (by the sword), and a Christian serves in either. Rulers may not command faith, and subjects must not revolt. The Augsburg Confession (art. 16) says Christians must obey 'except when commanded to sin,' when 'we must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). In 1934 some Lutheran and Reformed churches joined in the Barmen Declaration against the Nazi state's claim over the church.

Calvin teaches obedience to rulers, even bad ones, but adds that 'lesser magistrates' appointed to protect the people may restrain a tyrant (Institutes 4.20.31). The Westminster Confession (ch. 23) teaches obedience 'for conscience' sake.' Karl Barth, a Reformed theologian, drafted much of the Barmen Declaration.

The Thirty-Nine Articles (art. 37) assign the monarch 'the chief government' under God, and the 1571 Homily Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion taught that even a wicked ruler is not to be resisted by force; Anglicans later divided over that teaching, especially in 1688.

The Schleitheim Confession (1527, art. 6) holds that the 'sword is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ,' and that Christians do not serve as magistrates or bear the sword; they pay taxes and submit in all but what violates conscience. Many Mennonite and Brethren groups still hold this.

Roger Williams argued that the magistrate's power is civil only and that no government may rule the conscience (The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution, 1644). The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 17) says God alone is Lord of the conscience, and the 1689 Confession (ch. 24) teaches subjection to lawful magistrates.

title: Welcome Without Judging
sum: Chapter 14 begins the long case that runs to 15:13: the "strong" and the "weak" in Rome must welcome one another. The strong eat anything and treat all days alike; the weak eat only vegetables, avoid wine, and keep certain days. Paul does not say who is right on the facts, though he says he is convinced that nothing is common in itself (14:14). His whole interest is in how the two sides treat each other. The strong must not scorn the weak, and the weak must not judge the strong, for each stands before the Lord.

The reasons come in waves: God has welcomed both; the Lord is each person's master; we will all stand before God's judgment seat; love forbids ruining a brother over food; and the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. The chapter ends with a hard sentence: whatever does not come from faith is sin.
readings: As a quarrel between Jews and Gentiles
The traditional reading sees Jewish believers who kept food laws and holy days, and Gentile believers who did not. Paul takes the side of liberty in principle and of love in practice.
As a wider problem of scruples

Another reading sees a mixed group of the over-careful, Jews and Gentiles, who worried about meat from pagan markets, wine for idols, or fasts, and sees Paul's teaching as a rule for how Christians should live with differences of conscience.

views.H: Food was bound up with religion in the Roman world: meat in the market often came from temple sacrifices, and wine was poured out to the gods at many meals. Jews had developed ways of avoiding this, including vegetables and water (Daniel 1; Tobit 1:10-11; Josephus, Life 13-14). In Rome the Jewish community was large, and after the Claudian expulsion returning Jewish believers met a church that had become mainly Gentile. Some scholars (Donfried, Wedderburn) place the strong-weak tension here.
views.C: Who the weak were is the main critical question: Jewish believers (the older view), Jews outside the Christian community (Nanos), or mixed ascetics (Reasoner). Paul does not use the words Jew or Gentile until 15:7-13, and the practices he lists (vegetables, wine, days) are not exactly those of the Torah, which complicates the view that the weak simply kept the law. The relation of this chapter to 1 Corinthians 8 to 10 is also discussed: Paul is much milder here than there about meat sacrificed to idols.
views.L: The chapter is a diatribe-like exchange with two imagined parties ("you, why do you judge?... you, why do you despise?", 14:10). Paul keeps the strong and the weak in balance by turns, and he uses first-person plural ("we live ... we die", 14:7-8) to include himself. The turn at 14:13 ("let us no longer judge") moves from one argument to another. The last verse (14:23) sums up with the single word "faith," which Paul used in 1:17 for the heart of the gospel.
views.J: Paul says nothing in this chapter about Jews no longer keeping kashrut or the Sabbath. Readers who place Paul within Judaism (Nanos, Fredriksen and others) note that his language is about what the strong may do and what they should avoid doing for the weak, not about what Jews must give up. The word "common" (14:14) is the Jewish term for what is ordinary and so not holy. Orthodox Judaism keeps both the dietary laws and the Sabbath as Torah commands for Jews.
views.T: The chapter is a basic text for the church's thinking about liberty and conscience. Augustine used 14:23 for the virtues of those without faith, and Aquinas for the binding force of conscience. Luther's "On the Freedom of a Christian" (1520) puts the two sides in one line, a Christian is free lord of all and servant of all, much the shape of Paul's argument here. Calvin takes Paul's rule as the basis for "things indifferent" (adiaphora) in the church. The Sabbath and the food laws, as the cards below show, are two places where churches differ.

deep.b:
Paul gives a chain of reasons why the strong must not despise and the weak must not judge:

  1. God has welcomed that person (14:3). Any ranking contradicts God's welcome.
  2. Each stands before his own master (14:4). A slave's master, not his fellow slave, judges him.
  3. All live and die for the Lord (14:7-9). Christ died and lived to be Lord of both the dead and the living, so everyone belongs to him.
  4. All will stand before God (14:10-12). The final judgment is God's, so no one else has the right.
  5. Love forbids ruining a brother for whom Christ died (14:15), and "the kingdom of God is not food and drink" (14:17).

None of the five tells the weak that their view is right or wrong. They tell both sides what their view is worth in the face of God.

Paul treats a similar problem in 1 Corinthians 8 to 10, where meat sacrificed to idols is the matter. There he allows eating but, in a temple meal, forbids it as fellowship with demons (1 Corinthians 10:14-22). Here he mentions no idols, and the language is closer to Jewish purity ("common"). Some scholars think the situations differ; others think Paul gives the same advice with the idol issue in the background. These letters are not yet written on this site, so this part is a pointer.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 8; 1 Corinthians 10:23-33; Galatians 4:8-11; Colossians 2:16-23; Mark 7:1-23; Acts 10:9-16; Acts 15:19-29; Isaiah 45:23; Philippians 2:10-11; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Daniel 1:8-16; Leviticus 11

settings.to: The strong, who eat anything, and the weak, who eat vegetables and keep days, in the Roman house churches; addressed one party at a time, with 'you' for each
settings.why: To make two groups in the same house churches welcome each other without a verdict on who is right. Paul's own view is on the side of the strong (14:14), but he asks them to give up their liberty where it harms the weak, and asks the weak not to condemn.
settings.readers: Roman believers with different practices over food, wine and holy days. The Jewish returnees and the Gentile majority of the city may be behind it.
views: The weak are Jewish Christians who keep Torah customs; the strong are Gentile Christians (the traditional view; Cranfield, Dunn).
The weak are a group of the over-careful including Gentiles, concerned for ritual purity or for avoiding idol food (Reasoner).
The 'weak' are Jews in the synagogues who had not accepted Jesus (Nanos), and Paul warns the Gentile believers against scorning them.

traditions.q: Is 'one day above another' (14:5) about the Sabbath, and are Christians bound to keep the seventh day?
views: Sunday, the Lord's Day, took the place of the Sabbath. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ; the Sunday rest is a Christian duty grounded in the creation order and the resurrection (Catechism 2174-2176; John Paul II, Dies Domini).

Sunday is the Lord's Day, the 'eighth day' of the resurrection, and the center of the week. The old church canons forbid fasting on Saturday except Holy Saturday (Apostolic Canons, canon 64). The Orthodox do not teach a legal Sabbath.

The Sabbath command is not a law binding on Christians as such. Luther's Small Catechism teaches that the third commandment means that we should not despise preaching and God's word; the Augsburg Confession (art. 28) says Sunday is a church arrangement, not a necessity.

The Westminster Confession (21.7-8) teaches that one day in seven is a perpetual command, moved by Christ's resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord's Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept with rest. Calvin held that the ceremonial side of the Sabbath ended but its purpose of rest and worship remains.
Most Baptists keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, as in the Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 8). Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh day remains binding.
The seventh-day Sabbath is a creation gift and part of the Ten Commandments, binding on all; Romans 14:5 concerns the ceremonial feasts and fasts, not the weekly Sabbath (Fundamental Belief 20).

Jewish followers of Jesus keep the Sabbath as part of the Torah and the Jewish covenant, and many do so in Saturday services; Mark Kinzer and David Stern write of this as a Jewish calling. Congregations differ on whether Gentile believers are bound.

traditions.q: Does 'nothing is common in itself' (14:14) end the food laws of Leviticus 11 for Christians?
views: The ceremonial precepts of the Old Law, among them the food laws, ended with Christ; they pointed to him and are not binding (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 103-104; Catechism 1964). The Church's own days of fasting and abstinence are a different matter, a discipline of penance.

Christians are not bound by the food laws of Leviticus. The church does keep a strict discipline of fasting from meat and dairy on set days, as training in self-control and not because any food is unclean.
The Augsburg Confession (art. 26, 'Of the Distinction of Meats') teaches that rules about foods are not a way of earning grace, and that a Christian is free in them.

The Westminster Confession (19.3) teaches that the ceremonial laws were 'abrogated under the New Testament.' Romans 14:14 is among the proof texts for Christian freedom of conscience in such matters (ch. 20).

The distinction between clean and unclean meats was known before Moses (Genesis 7:2) and remains healthful guidance for believers, who abstain from pork and shellfish; Paul in Romans 14 concerns meat offered to idols and fasting, not Leviticus 11 (Fundamental Beliefs, 'Christian Behavior').

Jewish believers in Jesus may and often do keep kosher as part of their Jewish calling (Kinzer, Stern); on this reading Paul's words in Romans 14 ask the strong not to scorn them, and do not tell Jews to give up the Torah. Opinions differ on whether Gentile believers are bound.

title: Christ the Servant, and Paul's Plans
sum: Chapter 15 first finishes the case for welcome. Christ did not please himself, and he became a servant of the Jews to confirm God's promises to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles might also praise God for mercy. A chain of four quotations from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms shows Gentiles and Jews rejoicing together, and Paul prays that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace.

The second half looks forward. Paul describes his work as a priest's service for the Gentiles, says he has finished his work in the east from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and asks Rome to help him on to Spain. First he must carry the collection from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem. He asks for prayer that he will be rescued and that the gift will be accepted. (Acts 21 to 28 tells what followed.)
readings: As the end of the argument

Many commentators read 15:7-13 as the climax of the whole letter: Jews and Gentiles are called to praise God together, since Christ has confirmed the promises to Israel and extended mercy to the nations.
As Paul's business letter
Others stress that 15:14-33 shows why Paul wrote: he needs a base in Rome for Spain, he is about to take a risk in Jerusalem, and he wants a united church behind him.

views.H: In the winter of 56-57 Paul was in Corinth (Acts 20:2-3: "He stayed three months"), about to leave for Jerusalem with the collection, then for Rome and Spain. His arrival in Jerusalem about Pentecost of 57 led to his arrest (Acts 21:27-36), two years in Caesarea (Acts 24:27), and the voyage to Rome, probably about 60-61 (Acts 27 to 28). Whether he ever reached Spain is not known. The collection was a large undertaking: delegates from Macedonia, Galatia and Asia accompanied it (Acts 20:4); that list names no delegate from Achaia.
views.C: Scholars use 15:14-33 as the main evidence of why Paul wrote (the 'Romans debate'): to prepare for Spain (Jewett), to answer Jewish-Gentile tension (Wedderburn, Donfried), to explain his gospel before Jerusalem (Jervell). The text of the end of Romans is complicated: Papyrus 46 puts the doxology after 15:33 (see the entry there), and some think Romans circulated in a shorter form ending at 15:33 (Gamble).
views.L: 15:1-13 closes the weak-strong argument with Christ as the model and the four-fold chain of Scripture (Psalm 18, Deuteronomy 32, Psalm 117, Isaiah 11). It echoes the opening of the letter by returning to the Gentiles' obedience and the root of Jesse (1:3-5). The second half is a personal section with the form of a letter's travel plan (an 'apostolic parousia').
views.J: Verse 8 is crucial: Christ became a servant of the circumcised so that God's truthfulness to the patriarchs would be shown. Jewish and Christian readers of Romans after the Holocaust have drawn on this verse, with 11:28-29, to reject the idea that the church replaced Israel (Nostra Aetate 4). Paul's picture of himself as a priest offering up the Gentiles (15:16) echoes Isaiah 66:20, a prophecy of the nations coming to Zion. The collection is also a Jewish duty of care for the poor of Jerusalem that Gentiles are privileged to share.
views.T: Clement of Rome (1 Clement 5:7) is the first to say Paul reached 'the limit of the west.' The Muratorian Fragment says he went to Spain, and later tradition has him there. Calvin comments on 15:4 that Scripture is given for the instruction of all believers. In the Roman lectionary and in Anglican practice, 15:4-13 is the reading for the Second Sunday of Advent.

deep.b:
Putting together Acts and the letters gives this sequence (dates approximate):

  • About 53-56 Paul works in Ephesus (Acts 19), writes to Corinth, and collects money from the Gentile churches.
  • Winter 56-57 Three months in Greece, mostly Corinth (Acts 20:2-3); Romans is written.
  • Spring 57 The journey to Jerusalem with delegates (Acts 20:4 to Acts 21:17).
  • Pentecost 57 Paul reaches Jerusalem; Jerusalem leaders ask him to join in a temple vow (Acts 21:17-26); he is seized in the temple (Acts 21:27-36).
  • 57-59 Two years in custody in Caesarea (Acts 24:27).
  • About 60-61 The voyage to Rome (Acts 27 to Acts 28:14-16); two years under guard in Rome (Acts 28:30-31).

Acts never tells whether the collection was accepted. Whether Paul left Rome for Spain, as 15:24 plans, is not known (see the note at 15:24).

Paul's chain of Scripture contains one text from each part of the Hebrew Bible: Psalm 18:49 (Writings), Deuteronomy 32:43 (the Law), Psalm 117:1 (Writings) and Isaiah 11:10 (Prophets). Each has the key word "Gentiles" or "peoples." The chain moves from Gentiles joining Israel in praise to Gentiles praising alone, and ends with the Davidic king who rules them. Notice the Greek form of Isaiah 11:10: it says the Gentiles will "hope" in him, where this site's Plain of the Hebrew text says "nations will come seeking him." For the Hebrew and the Greek see the notes.

echoes: Psalm 69:9; Psalm 18:49; Deuteronomy 32:43; Psalm 117:1; Isaiah 11:10; Isaiah 52:15; Isaiah 66:19-20; Galatians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; 2 Corinthians 8 to 9; Acts 20:1-4; Acts 21:17-36; Acts 24:17; Acts 28:30-31; 1 Clement 5:7

settings.what: Christ's example and the call to welcome
settings.to: The strong first ("we who are strong"), then the whole Roman church, Jews and Gentiles
settings.when: as the conclusion of the strong-weak section begun at 14:1
settings.why: To ground the welcome in Christ's own choice not to please himself, and in God's promise to the patriarchs and the nations. The Scripture chain shows that Gentile praise belongs in the plan of the Hebrew Bible.
settings.readers: Roman believers who must live together across the lines of strong and weak and Jew and Gentile.

settings.what: Paul's ministry, collection and travel plans
settings.to: The whole Roman church, whom he has not visited
settings.when: from Corinth, as he is about to leave for Jerusalem
settings.why: To explain why he has written boldly to a church he did not found, to tell them about his priestly service to the Gentiles, to announce a visit and the trip to Spain, and to ask for prayer for the risky trip to Jerusalem with the collection.
settings.readers: A church to whom Paul is almost unknown, apart from those he knows by name (chapter 16). The announcement asks for their support in a western mission.
views: The main purpose of the letter is to win Rome's help for the Spanish mission (Jewett).
Paul wrote partly to rehearse his gospel before facing Jerusalem and to gain the prayers of a major church (Jervell).
The letter is a considered statement of his gospel for its own sake, and the plans are secondary (many older commentators).

title: Names, a Warning and a Doxology
sum: Chapter 16 is the longest list of greetings in any of Paul's letters. It opens by commending Phoebe, a servant and patron of the church at Cenchreae, who almost certainly carried the letter to Rome. Then Paul greets about two dozen people by name, from Prisca and Aquila, who risked their lives for him, to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus. Among them are Andronicus and Junia, "outstanding among the apostles," and a remarkable number of women who "toil in the Lord."

A sharp warning against people who cause divisions (16:17-20) breaks in, and the letter closes with greetings from Paul's companions in Corinth, including Tertius, who wrote it down. A verse that many Bibles print at 16:24 is missing from the oldest manuscripts. The closing doxology (16:25-27) stands at the end in the earliest complete manuscripts, but in other copies it stands elsewhere, and it ties back to the opening words, "the obedience of faith."
readings: As a map of the early church

The list shows who made up the Roman church: Jews and Gentiles, slaves and freed people, women and men, small house groups, with a few of means. Paul names more women in this chapter than in any other letter.
As an argument about unity
Others see the greetings as Paul's last argument. By naming Jews (relatives), Gentiles, women, slaves and members of the emperor's households in one list, he shows the unity of the church in action.

views.H: The names are those of ordinary people of the city of Rome: many are slave or freedman names (Hermes, Urbanus, Nereus), common in the inscriptions and the burial places (columbaria) of Rome's households, and two groups are tied to great households, Aristobulus and Narcissus. Prisca and Aquila had returned to Rome, probably after Claudius died in 54. At least five groups met in separate homes. Paul writes from Corinth, where Gaius hosted the church and Erastus held a city office.
views.C: Whether chapter 16 belonged to the letter sent to Rome is a major question. A minority (T. W. Manson, 1948, and others) have argued it was a note to Ephesus, because Paul would hardly know so many people in a city he never visited. Most scholars today (Gamble, Dunn, Jewett) hold that it belongs: Paul knew people who had moved to Rome, and a list of names would give him standing. Further critical discussion concerns 16:17-20 (possibly a later insertion), the missing verse 16:24, and the doxology of 16:25-27: its position in the manuscripts, its style, and whether Paul wrote it.
views.L: The chapter is built as a letter's close: commendation (16:1-2), greetings (16:3-16), warning (16:17-20), greetings from the senders (16:21-23), doxology (16:25-27). The word "greet" is repeated in nearly every verse of 16:3-16 and the phrase "in the Lord" or "in Christ" fills the list. The doxology picks up key words from 1:1-5: "my good news," "the prophets," "the obedience of faith," and "all the Gentiles."
views.J: Several of the people are plainly Jews: Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, Herodion and the other "relatives" (a word that means fellow Jews, as in 9:3). Greeting Jews and Gentiles in the same church, in the same list, is Paul's argument for the unity of 9 to 11 and 14 to 15. The name Herodion and the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus point to Jewish and imperial circles. Paul calls himself and his friends coworkers in a movement that is still, for him, the fulfillment of the prophets (16:26).
views.T: Chrysostom marvels at the greetings and at Junia's title of apostle, praising the devotion of the women. Origen sees in Phoebe a woman 'set in the ministry of the church.' The place of the doxology exercised Origen, who knew of copies with the doxology at two places and said that Marcion cut the end of the letter. The church has used 16:25-27 as a doxology in its worship ever since. The question of Phoebe and Junia is central to the modern debate over the ordination of women (see the card).

deep.h: Chapter 16: to Rome or to Ephesus?
deep.b:
The list of greetings has raised a question since the 1800s. Paul had never been to Rome (1:10-13; 15:22-24), so why does he know so many people there? Two views:

A note to Ephesus. Some scholars (T. W. Manson in 1948 and others) have held that chapter 16 was a separate letter, or a copy of Romans with a different last chapter, sent to Ephesus, where Prisca and Aquila had been (Acts 18:19; 1 Corinthians 16:19), where Epaenetus was a convert (16:5), and which Paul knew well. Arguments: so many greetings, the warning of 16:17-20 (not like the rest of the letter), and some manuscripts which have the doxology at 15:33.

Belongs to Rome. Most scholars (Gamble, Dunn, Jewett, Moo) hold that the chapter belongs where it stands. Arguments: people moved to Rome from all over the empire and from Paul's circle (Prisca and Aquila had just done it); the list gives Paul his link to a church he does not know; the names (Aristobulus, Narcissus, the imperial freed names) fit Rome; and every manuscript of Romans has the chapter. This letter is Paul's way of saying he knows this church and its members.

The question touches the doxology and the missing 16:24, because the shorter forms of Romans in the manuscripts either end at 14:23 or at 15:33.

The closing doxology (16:25-27) stands in different places in the manuscripts. As reported by Metzger and the apparatus of NA28:

  • After 16:23, at the end (the position in NA28 and Tyndale House, and in the KJV): reported in Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Ephraemi (04), Claromontanus (06) and a large number of other manuscripts, Papyrus 61 (about AD 700, reported), and in the Latin Vulgate.
  • After 14:23: the great majority of Byzantine manuscripts, including L and Psi.
  • After both 14:23 and 16:23: Alexandrinus (02) and a few others.
  • After 15:33: Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), the oldest copy of Romans.
  • Missing: Boernerianus and Augiensis are reported to omit it; Marcion's text of Romans, according to Origen, ended at 14:23.

Origen, in his commentary on Romans (in Rufinus' Latin, 10.43), says Marcion cut the letter off at 14:23 and removed the doxology; he adds that in other copies the doxology comes right after 14:23, and in others at the end.

Why the movement? Harry Gamble (1977) argued that Romans circulated in several forms, a 14-chapter form ending at 14:23 with the doxology, a 15-chapter form ending at 15:33, and the full 16-chapter form, and that the shorter forms were not made by Marcion, but earlier. Others think Marcion or a reader cut the end, and the doxology was used to close the shortened letter.

Is it Paul's? It has features that have led many scholars to doubt it: a long, liturgical sentence which does not finish smoothly, the phrases "the eternal God" and "the only wise God," and the language of a mystery "kept in silence" now revealed (as in Colossians and Ephesians). Other scholars point to the echoes of the letter's opening ("my good news," "the obedience of faith" in 1:5 and 16:26, "all the Gentiles") and judge that Paul wrote it or a close helper did. Matters stand open. The Plain translates it where NA28 and Tyndale House print it. The STEPBible edition table marks the SBLGNT with 16:24 but not with 16:25-27, so editions disagree even about what the "standard" text includes.

Of the 25 people named in 16:1-15, eight are women: Phoebe, Prisca, Mary, Junia, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis and Julia, and two more women are named only as relatives (Rufus' mother and Nereus' sister). Of these, Phoebe is called a servant (or deacon) and a patron, Prisca is a coworker named before her husband, Junia is "outstanding among the apostles," and four are said to have "toiled" (Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis). The list matters in two ways: as history, it shows women with real roles in the early churches; and in later arguments about what women may do in the church. The churches read it very differently (see the card at the end of this chapter).

echoes: Acts 18:1-4, 18-26; Acts 20:2-4; 1 Corinthians 1:14; 1 Corinthians 16:19-20; Mark 15:21; Philippians 4:22; Colossians 4:7-18; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; Genesis 3:15; Romans 1:1-7; Romans 11:25

settings.when: as part of the letter's close, with Phoebe in all likelihood the one carrying the letter
settings.why: To introduce the bearer of the letter to a church that did not know her, and to ask for hospitality and help for her business in the city. Such letters of recommendation were common in the Roman world.
settings.readers: House churches who would welcome a traveling believer on her word. Her title, 'servant of the church in Cenchreae,' gave her standing.

settings.to: About two dozen named people and their house groups, Jews and Gentiles, slaves, freed people and householders
settings.when: at the end of the letter
settings.why: To show that Paul has a relationship with the Roman church through many individuals, to honor co-workers, and to remind the several house groups that they belong to one body. The 'holy kiss' marks the whole church as one family.
settings.readers: Roman house churches, at least five groups.
views: Paul knew people who had moved to Rome; the list is a natural way to link him to a church he did not found (most commentators).
The chapter is a note to Ephesus (T. W. Manson and others); see the deep dive.

settings.what: A warning against those who cause divisions
settings.to: The Roman believers as a whole
settings.when: at the end of the letter, as he adds a final caution
settings.why: To warn against teachers who split the church, seeking their own gain by smooth talk, and to encourage obedience to the teaching the Romans had been taught. He ends with the promise that the God of peace will crush Satan.
settings.readers: Believers who might be taken in by clever teachers, and who had already shown tensions between strong and weak.
views: Some scholars (for example Jewett) judge it post-Pauline.

settings.what: Greetings from Paul's companions in Corinth
settings.by: Timothy, Lucius, Jason, Sosipater, Tertius (the scribe), Gaius, Erastus and Quartus
settings.why: To join the Corinthian circle to the Roman one, and to show who is with Paul. The scribe Tertius adds his own greeting.
settings.readers: The Roman church, who would know some of these people by reputation.

settings.by: Paul, or someone close to him (debated)
settings.to: God, in the hearing of the Roman church
settings.when: at the close of the letter, or at one of the other places where manuscripts put it
settings.why: To close the letter with praise that returns to its opening themes: the good news, the Scriptures, the nations, and the obedience of faith.
settings.readers: Roman believers, who would have heard the letter read aloud, probably in the house churches.
views: Held by a number of commentators, who point to the echoes of the letter's opening (the good news, the Scriptures, the nations, the obedience of faith in 1:1-5).
Held by many critical scholars, who point to the doxology's moving position in the manuscripts, its long liturgical sentence, and language close to Colossians and Ephesians.
Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible commentary reads Junia as a woman and as an apostle in the wide sense of a missionary sent out by a church, not one of the Twelve.
Chrysostom takes the name as a woman's and marvels that she was counted worthy of the title of apostle. The Orthodox calendar remembers Andronicus and Junia among the apostles on 17 May.

Divided. Eldon Epp and Linda Belleville argue that 'outstanding among the apostles' means Junia was herself an apostle. Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace argue that it means 'well known to the apostles'. Both sides agree the name is a woman's.

traditions.q: May women be ordained to lead churches (16:1)?
views: Only baptized men are ordained as priests and bishops (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994; Catechism 1577). Women serve in many other roles. Whether women could be ordained as deacons, as Phoebe was perhaps, has been studied by commissions set up by Pope Francis (2016 and 2020) without a decision.

Only men are ordained to the priesthood and episcopate. The early church had a recognized order of women deacons (deaconesses), with Phoebe as the usual precedent, and there have been recent moves to revive it.
Divided. The Church of Sweden opened ordination to women in 1958. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod does not ordain women and appeals to 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 and 1 Timothy 2:12.
Divided. The Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. opened ordination as ministers to women in 1956; the Presbyterian Church in America reserves the offices of pastor and elder for men.
Divided by province. The Episcopal Church in the United States opened the priesthood to women in 1976 and the Church of England in 1993 (first ordinations 1994); other provinces do not ordain women.
The Methodist Church in the United States granted women full clergy rights in 1956.

Divided, since Baptist congregations and conventions govern themselves. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 6) limits the office of pastor to men 'as qualified by Scripture'; other Baptist bodies ordain women.

Most Pentecostal bodies, such as the Assemblies of God, ordain women, pointing to the gifts of the Spirit that Peter cites from Joel (Acts 2:17-18) and to the women of Romans 16; a few smaller bodies do not.
Many Mennonite bodies ordain women; see the Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), article 15, on ministry and leadership.
Friends have no ordained clergy; women have spoken and led in ministry among them since the 1600s (Margaret Fell, Women's Speaking Justified, 1666).
